Window and desktop integration

Clicking another app’s icon on the Linux desktop, rather than its icon on the Android home screen, launches that app in a separate, fixed-size window with its own entry in the Linux desktop taskbar. Only one app can still run at a time; they cannot run simultaneously. Switching app windows pauses the other app: a game’s screen freezes, for example, or Youtube stops playing. These apps cannot use the notification shade, and pressing Back automatically closes the app window without fully stopping the app.

If you enable “multi-window mode” (see below), the Waydroid icon disappears from the Linux desktop. Apps launched from the Linux desktop then have resizable windows and can run simultaneously without pausing when you switch apps. Clicking the close button or pressing Back closes the app window without fully stopping the app.

Waydroid’s text clipboard integration and input-method integration are separate features. You can install a suitable input method in Android; you are not limited to Gboard. Availability of the host’s input method depends on graphics/input integration.

6. Install an ARM translator to fix app crashes

Computers with an ARM architecture can skip this step. Most computers use x86, while many mobile games provide only ARM APKs, so software is needed to translate ARM instructions into x86 instructions. How can you tell whether an app is ARM-only? Without an ARM translator installed by default, Google Play may not show certain apps. Alternatively, after installing an APK, use Package Manager to check whether the app includes /lib/x86_64 libraries. If it has only ARM libraries, it will crash on launch and needs an ARM translator. Available ARM translators include Intel’s “libhoudini” and Google’s “libndk”; both are proprietary software. Some community advice suggests choosing by CPU vendor, but that is not a proven performance guarantee. Image versions, instruction sets, and individual apps especially need real-world testing. Some apps may work with one translator but not the other, so test different combinations. Do not install both ARM translators at the same time. To switch to the other one, run the script below, select Remove to remove the old translator, and then install the new one.

Run the script, use Space to select libhoudini or libndk, then press Enter to install the ARM translator. ARM translators are tied strictly to their Android version and must not be mixed across versions.

8. Run duplicate apps and multiple apps simultaneously

Waydroid is not designed to run multiple instances, so you cannot use separate instances to log in to two accounts in the same app at once. However, you can use Shelter’s work-profile feature to run two copies of an app in a single Android system. By design, Waydroid adds an icon for each Android app to the Linux desktop’s application list after its APK is installed. Launching apps from these icons lets you run multiple apps, but “multi-window mode” must be enabled for two or more apps to run “simultaneously.” What if an app refuses to run windowed in multi-window mode and insists on full-screen? Make use of your desktop environment’s virtual desktops. GNOME, KDE Plasma, Hyprland, and COSMIC all provide virtual desktops, also called workspaces. If an app fills the entire current virtual desktop when launched, switch to the next virtual desktop before launching another app. Each workspace can then run its own app.
9. Share a directory between Linux and Waydroid

After Waydroid starts, its data is in ~/.local/share/waydroid/data/media/0/. This is Android’s internal storage and requires root privileges to access. With KDE Dolphin file manager 6.0 or later, you can request root privileges to access Android’s files. Alternatively, access files by mounting a directory with ordinary permissions. To avoid affecting other files, I recommend creating a dedicated shared folder named WaydroidShared on both sides. Use mount to mount Linux’s ~/WaydroidShared onto the WaydroidShared folder inside Waydroid: You can also transfer files wirelessly with ADB commands. Find Waydroid’s IP address under Android system settings → About.

13. Adjust app volume

Open Android system settings → Sound to adjust the volume. Physical keys cannot control volume inside the Android container, so install a separate volume-control app. Add it as a widget on the Android home screen, or use Sound Quick Settings to add a volume-control button to Android’s notification shade. The Linux desktop’s volume-control panel, such as pavucontrol, can mute Waydroid’s output separately. Waydroid can also access the Linux microphone, so Android apps should be able to record audio normally. Microphone volume can likewise be adjusted in pavucontrol. If multiple apps are running and you want to mute a particular app, the MixedAudio feature in ShizuTools is recommended. Android’s multitasking screen has a screenshot button for individual apps. There is no Linux-side shortcut to trigger the Android hardware-key screenshot action, so use a Linux screenshot tool. Alternatively, install Screenshot Tile to add a native screenshot button to Android’s notification shade.
15. Prevent crashes caused by app detection of root or an emulator

Sometimes an app refuses to install or crashes because it considers your device unsafe, rather than because of ARM translation. Waydroid cannot pass even the most basic Play Integrity API level, so some apps refuse to run. Apps requiring DRM also cannot play their content. The solution is more complicated: you might install Magisk to hide root or spoof the device model.
